title: He Said, “If You Loved Me, You Would.” What If Your Boyfriend Doesn't Want to Wait?
paragraphs:
He Said, “If You Loved Me, You Would.” What If Your Boyfriend Doesn't Want to Wait?
When love asks you to compromise your obedience, is it still love? The answer may change not only your relationship—but your eternity.
There are conversations that leave bruises no one else can see.
But because someone you deeply love slowly convinced you that your convictions were unreasonable.
And perhaps the hardest one of all...
Those words have shattered countless hearts—not because they were loud, but because they sounded believable.
Many Christian women and men never planned to walk away from purity.
They simply wanted to keep someone from walking away from them.
That is how compromise usually begins.
Fear that obedience might cost too much.
But Scripture asks a question far deeper than, "Will he stay?"
Will you remain faithful to Christ even if he doesn't?
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Because purity was never primarily about protecting your body.
It has always been about protecting your worship.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly use the word קָדוֹשׁ (qādôš)—"holy," meaning set apart, belonging exclusively to God.
Holiness is not merely avoiding sin.
You are not merely someone trying to stay "good."
If you belong to Christ, you are already His.
"You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body." (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)
In the Greek text, Paul writes:
οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν... ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς. δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.
"You are not your own...for you were purchased with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body."
The verb ἠγοράσθητε (ēgorásthēte) literally means to be bought from the marketplace.
At Calvary, Christ paid with His blood what no amount of human effort could ever repay.
How then can someone who did not purchase you demand ownership over what belongs to Jesus?
Because culture teaches us that love earns access.
Jesus teaches us that covenant comes before intimacy.
The modern world often confuses desire with love.
The Greek language offers several words connected to love.
But when Scripture repeatedly describes God's love, it emphasizes ἀγάπη (agápē)—self-giving, sacrificial love that seeks another person's highest good before personal satisfaction.
If someone continually pressures you to sin against God for their own gratification...
Real love never asks someone to dishonor the One who created them.
"If you love Me, you will keep My commandments." (John 14:15)
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολάς μου τηρήσετε.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
"If you love Me, you'll feel emotional."
"If you love Me, you'll attend church."
"If you love Me, you'll post Christian content."
The word τηρήσετε (tērēsete) means to guard, preserve, watch over carefully, treasure.
Obedience is love protecting what it treasures.
Yet Jesus never promised obedience would always preserve earthly relationships.
Sometimes obedience exposes which relationships were never built upon Christ.
A boyfriend who truly desires to honor God should become your greatest encouragement toward holiness—not your greatest temptation.
But there is an enormous difference between struggling against temptation and recruiting someone else into it.
The Greek begins with remarkable urgency:
Notice what Paul does not say.
Because some victories happen only when you stop standing where the battle is strongest.
But Scripture never teaches us to plan our sin around future forgiveness.
"Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!"
Grace is not permission to keep walking toward the cliff.
Grace is God's hand pulling us away from it.
One of the greatest scandals in history is not merely that humanity sinned.
It is that the perfectly holy Son of God willingly entered our scandal.
But because His mercy was greater.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
None of us comes to Jesus impressive.
That is why our ministry says:
The Gospel does not erase your past by pretending it never happened.
It transforms your future because Jesus paid for your past.
Perhaps you've already crossed boundaries you deeply regret.
Maybe tears have become your nightly prayer.
Hear the words of David after his own devastating moral failure:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God..." (Psalm 51:10)
"A clean heart create in me, O God."
The verb בְּרָא (bara') is the same creative verb used in Genesis 1:1.
David wasn't asking God to repair his old heart.
He was asking for something only the Creator could do.
If your boyfriend truly loves Jesus, your obedience should increase his respect—not diminish his affection.
If your decision to honor Christ causes him to leave, painful as it may be, he has revealed something invaluable: he loved access to your body more than he loved your soul.
You deserve someone who will kneel beside you in prayer before he ever reaches for your hand in temptation.
Someone who wants to help you arrive at marriage with gratitude instead of regret.
Someone who understands that holiness is not old-fashioned—it is beautiful because it reflects Christ.
The world may laugh at purity.
Everything changed because Jesus walked out of the tomb.
The resurrection forever proves that God specializes in rewriting endings people thought were final.
If your story has already been marked by compromise, shame, or brokenness, your identity does not have to remain there.
Christ still receives those who return.
His grace is still greater than your greatest scandal.
If this article stirred your heart, don't let the conviction end with a quiet scroll.
If you desire to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel ministry is one practical way to participate in making Christ known (Philippians 1:3–5; 4:15–17).
One decision made in obedience today can become the testimony that changes generations tomorrow.
